Economics in this domain takes certain specific features of it into account, including our dependence on nature and the uncertainties this brings with it, our need for access to food and water, spatial considerations, and the failures of the market as a mechanism for allocation and distribution. This brings governance issues to the fore, the more so in view of the numerous policy interventions in this domain and the role of civil society groups. Economics in Wageningen therefore focuses on other social institutions than the market, and with a feel for the technical and nature-related aspects of the domain. It has built up a tradition of economic research of direct relevance to public policy, both national and international.
The BSc programme Economics and Governance covers the general principles of economics as well as offering specialized courses in economics and governance tailored to issues in agriculture, the environment, natural resources and development, both in Europe and elsewhere. Students are only allowed to start with their thesis writing after the successful completion of the Assessment part.
a) The assessment assists students in developing a clear view on their personality, characteristics and potential. Using the outcomes of an aptitude test students start thinking about their career in an early stage of the academic program. This will strengthen their ability to make proper choices in study programs and focus from year 3 on. They will visit an alumnus working in their field of interest for a reality 'check'. Students discuss, based on acquired insights, a well explained study plan with the study advisor.
b) The BSc thesis
The BSc thesis can be written under supervision of the staff of the chair groups: AEP, DEC, ENP, ENR, PAP, RHI, or UEC.
The student has to study (by means of a literature review or empirical research) a subject within the field of the major and prove to have sufficient knowledge to critically analyse and summarize the given subject. He/she must also be able to clearly communicate the findings in writing and by oral presentation. The subject will be determined in consultation with the thesis supervisor. The student has to define the research problem and formulate research questions in a proper way, deal with the logistics of carrying out such an individual research project, plan and schedule the different activities in a decent way, and present the results in writing in a clearly organized report.","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

Over

Geloof jij in een wereld waarin economie en duurzaamheid écht samengaan? Wil jij meer leren over economische thema’s die impact hebben op samenleving, milieu en internationale handel?  In deze studie leer je dat economie niet alleen gaat om winst maken. Met slim doordacht beleid geef jij de toekomst vorm. Denk bijvoorbeeld aan de energietransitie, innovatieve landbouw, afvalvermindering of gezonde voeding voor iedereen.

 

Benieuwd? Kom het zelf ervaren tijdens een proefstudeerdag.

Proefstuderen

Wat maakt deze opleiding uniek?

Economie én duurzaam beleid

Unieke combinatie van economische en bestuurskundige wetenschappen met nadruk op duurzaamheid. 

Je kent verschillende invalshoeken

Een mooie combinatie van economie en bestuurskunde en natuur- en klimaatvakken zodat je de verschillende invalshoeken kent en ook die verschillende ’talen’ spreekt.

Veel keuzevrijheid in specialisatie

Tijdens de opleiding leer je welke onderwerpen en richtingen bij jou passen. Je krijgt veel ruimte om je kennis te verdiepen of verbreden.

Ruim aanbod aan banen

De overheid stimuleert organisaties om duurzamer te handelen. Met de opleiding 
Economie en Beleid op zak ben je een waardevolle gesprekspartner en verbinder voor organisaties die verder kijken dan winstmaximalisatie.

Dit ga je leren

Jouw focus

Met verschillende brillen op onderzoek je hoe economie de wereld om ons heen beïnvloedt. Je kijkt bijvoorbeeld naar hoe steden en het platteland beter kunnen samenwerken of hoe we voedsel op een slimme en eerlijke manier kunnen produceren, in Nederland, Europa en wereldwijd. 

Dit ga je leren

  • Je krijgt inzicht in economische systemen.  
  • Je leert het analyseren van data en cijfers.  
  • Je komt alles te weten over toekomstgericht economisch beleid.
  • Je richt je op de mooie combi van maatschappij en milieu.
  • Je combineert expertise op meerdere vakgebieden tot sterk beleid.
Ontvang de brochure
Belangrijk:
Deze opleiding bevat geen bedrijfseconomische vakken zoals accountancy. Maar je kunt die wel opnemen in je vrijekeuzeruimte.

Jouw vakken

Studieprogramma

In je eerste studiejaar leer je veel over economie Je maakt ook kennis met het vakgebied bestuurskunde en je leert onderzoek doen. Dat pas je meteen toe bij het vak Analyse van een probleemveld. Ook ontdek je de relatie tussen economie en beleid en pas je dat toe op diverse maatschappelijke thema’s waaronder duurzame voedselsystemen.

Bekijk alle vakken.

Na het eerste jaar is het tijd voor verdere verdieping in Econometrie, Micro-economie en EU-beleid. Je gaat je ook specialiseren door vakken te kiezen richting economie of beleid. En je volgt twee natuurwetenschappelijke vakken zodat je de brug kunt slaan naar het natuurwetenschappelijk domein en je je daar later mee kunt onderscheiden.

Bekijk alle vakken.

In jaar 3 schrijf je je thesis, volg je vakken over energietransitie en Industrial Organisation, en je vult  je vrijekeuzeruimte in met een minor of zelfgekozen vakken. 

Bekijk alle vakken.

De minor die je in het derde studiejaar kunt doen, kies je helemaal zelf. Denk bijvoorbeeld aan de educatieve minor waarmee je je tweedegraads bevoegdheid kunt halen. Of een minor in de richting van biobased sciences, data science, filosofie of supply chain analytics. Of je stelt zelf een minor samen (waarbij de studieadviseur jou kan helpen). Deze minor doe je in Nederland of in het buitenland. 

Bekijk een totaaloverzicht van alle minors bij WUR.

De studie bestaat uit:

  • Hoorcolleges: een docent behandelt klassikaal de lesstof.
  • Werkcolleges: je doet een individuele opdracht of een opdracht met een groepje.  
  • Practica: dit zijn vooral computerpractica waarin je werkt met economische en statistische modellen.
  • Probleemgestuurd Onderwijs (PGO): je werkt met een groep en een begeleider aan een casus die je moet oplossen.  
  • Zelfstudie: zelfstudie zit in je rooster, maar kun je ook zelf inplannen buiten je rooster.  

Bij WUR vinden we persoonlijke begeleiding en contact heel belangrijk. Daarom is het aantal begeleiders (docenten, studieadviseurs en -begeleiders) dat jou helpt bij het doorlopen van je studie een stuk groter dan bij andere universiteiten in Nederland. Daarmee maken we de kans dat je je studie succesvol afrondt groter. Ook geeft persoonlijke aandacht meer studieplezier.

Sommige bacheloropleidingen zijn vergelijkbaar. De belangrijkste verschillen hebben we voor je op een rijtje gezet:

  • Bachelor Bedrijfs- en Consumentenwetenschappen
    Verdiep je in de wereld van producenten en consumenten. Of het nu gaat om een zak chips of een Ipad, er komen strategische en tactische beslissingen kijken bij succesvolle innovaties. Wat wil de consument? In deze studie neem je de uitdaging aan om beide groepen bij elkaar te brengen in het traject van businessplan tot eindproduct.
  • Bachelor Gezondheid en Maatschappij
    Zet je in voor een gezonde maatschappij vanuit een sociaalwetenschappelijke invalshoek. Je leert dat gezondheid van mensen veel te maken heeft met hun leefstijl en leefomgeving.
  • Bachelor Internationale Ontwikkelingsstudie
    Werk aan actuele ontwikkelingsvraagstukken zoals armoedebestrijding, vluchtelingenstromen en voedselzekerheid. Je houdt je bezig met veranderingen in levensomstandigheden van mensen in ontwikkelingslanden en Europa.
  • Bachelor Environmental Sciences
    Voor het oplossen van milieu- en duurzaamheidsvraagstukken combineer je natuurwetenschappelijke kennis met technologische mogelijkheden en voor mens en maatschappij relevante aspecten. Je werkt in multidisciplinaire teams waarin jij je eigen inbreng hebt.

Benieuwd naar hoe deze studie het doet vergeleken met vergelijkbare studies op andere universiteiten? Check de cijfers op Studiekeuze123.

Je leven na deze bachelor

Na de bachelor

Je kunt onwijs veel kanten op. Denk o.a. aan een baan als:  

  • Consultant duurzaamheid of verantwoord ondernemen.
  • Onderzoeker bij een kennisinstelling of universiteit.
  • Data-analist of marktonderzoeker bij een planbureau zoals CPB of PBL.
  • Beleidsadviseur bij een ministerie, provincie of gemeente.
  • Beleidsmedewerker in een internationale organisatie zoals de VN of een 
    ambassade. 
  • Manager of beleidsmedewerker in de private sector, zoals bij een bank of 
    energiebedrijf.

In het alumniboekje lees je hoe afgestudeerden hun studie inzetten in de praktijk.

Veel studenten doen een master na hun bacheloropleiding. Hiermee krijg je nog meer kennis en vaardigheden mee. Deze masters sluiten mooi aan:  

  • Master Economics of Sustainability
  • Master Governance of Sustainability Transformations
  • Master International Development Studies
  • Master Biobased Sciences 

Natuurlijk kun je ook voor een andere Wageningse master gaan. Door in het derde jaar van je bachelor slim je keuzevakken te kiezen, sluit dat later moeiteloos aan op master waar je voor gaat. Je studieadviseur helpt je daarbij, zodat je zonder studievertraging verder kunt.  

Liever een master aan een andere universiteit of zelfs in het buitenland? Geen probleem, want met jouw WUR-bachelordiploma gaan wereldwijd deuren voor je open.

Handige info

  • Natuur & Techniek  
  • Natuur & Gezondheid  
  • Economie & Maatschappij  
  • Cultuur & Maatschappij (als je de vakken wiskunde A of wiskunde B in je pakket hebt)  
Andere toelatingsmogelijkheden

Ook als je geen vwo-opleiding hebt of wiskunde mist, zijn er mogelijkheden om deze studie te volgen.  Controleer of je met jouw vooropleiding toelaatbaar bent tot deze bacheloropleiding. Lees hieronder meer wat bij jou van toepassing is:  

  • Vwo-diploma nieuwe tweede fase
  • Hbo-diploma of hbo-propedeuse 
  • Uitzonderingen (Colloquium Doctum) 
  • Buitenlands diploma

Education of Agricultural Economics and Rural Policy

The Agricultural Economics and Rural Policy Group provides training on a wide range of interesting topics offered by experienced staff members. Students receive solid training providing them with the knowledge to address research questions in the area of economics and policies related to the bioeconomy, rural and regional development, institutional and organizational aspects, and quantitative economics. We highly encourage students to develop their own ideas to apply advanced theoretical methods and quantitative tools. We also support them in their scientific and professional career.

List of completed Msc theses

Internship

An internship Agricultural Economics and Rural Policy allows you to fully participate at an academic level in a government organisation (e.g. Ministry), political party, NGO, business or other organisation that is involved in agricultural and rural economics and policy. At the Agricultural Economics and Rural Policy Group writing your M.Sc. thesis in the Group is a prerequisite for doing an internship. However, exceptions are possible in some cases. Please note that your internship must always be approved by the internship coordinator dr. Dusan Drabik or supervisor from the academic staff.

The course has been completely revised compared with previous years. The renewed course engages you with economic, business and political actuality by means of weekly case studies.

Using six weekly case studies, you will deepen your understanding of both the cases themselves and the theories of institutional economics and economic organisation. The cases address contemporary issues in the political and economic landscape, including futures markets, real estate development, land tenure, and alternative food supply chains. They cover examples from both Western and non-Western countries. So, through the case studies, you will gain insight into the cases discussed and develop the ability to analyse and conceptualise real-world economic situations and policy dilemmas.

Institutional economics and economic organisation theory extend beyond traditional economic theories by placing human behaviour, individual characteristics, and institutional constraints at the centre of the analysis. They help explain why different organisational forms emerge to provide the goods and services we consume, how governments can design effective policies to encourage or discourage certain behaviours, and why firms and countries adopt different institutional arrangements and policy approaches.

The course 'The Economics of Agriculture, Food and Policy' gives an introduction to (mainly EU) agri-food policies and the analysis of their economic effects. Issues dealt with are the history and motives of EU agri-food policies; policy instruments frequently used at global scale and their effects on domestic and international food trade and markets as well as developing countries. Moreover, AEP21806 deals with the Common Agricultural Policy of the EU and its problems and reforms and core aspects of international agricultural trade negotiations. Also the relationships between agri-food policies and rural development, the environment, animal welfare, and food safety are discussed.

The course consists of lectures, practicals, preparing short presentations and the writing of a policy brief. Students compete with each other in government groups playing the simulation game AGRIPOL. AGRIPOL quantifies the complex effects of agri-food policy choices on food markets and national welfare of individual countries as well as the entire world. Students apply policy instruments and learn by own experience to what effects and international complications national policy decisions may lead. During the practicals, the (unforeseeable) effects of various policy changes are analysed in detail. In the policy brief, students analyse and reflect on one chosen agri-food policy problem in detail. In the presentations, students analyse their country’s food market and their policy decisions.

Recommended book covering most topics of the lecture: Oskam, Meester, Silvis (2011). EU policy for agriculture, food and rural areas. Wageningen Academic Publishers.
Additional facultative reading: A list of suggested readings for each lecture will be made available in Brightspace in the section ‘Course Documents/ Suggested reading and further literature hints’.

The central questions addressed by industrial organization are: (i) Is there market power? (ii) How do firms acquire and maintain market power? (iii) What are the implications of market power? (iv) Is there a role for public policy with regard to market power? This course takes a formal approach to analyzing the way firms make production and sales decisions and interact strategically with each other in the marketplace. Whereas microeconomics typically focuses on the extreme cases of monopoly and perfect competition, industrial organization is primarily concerned with the intermediate case of oligopoly, that is, competition between a few firms (more than one, as in monopoly, but not as many as in competitive markets). We will cover selected topics of industrial organization, including price discrimination, oligopoly, collusion and price wars, market structure, horizontal mergers, and vertical relations. We will illustrate these issues by using examples from agriculture and other sectors. Readings in the textbook will provide background and introduction to a variety of topics, many of which will be covered in class in greater depth. Exercises solved in class and problem sets will focus on formal analysis. The economics discipline has made great strides in developing tools that can help us understand, explain, and address the challenges currently facing our world. This introductory economics course introduces key tools and concepts such as strategic interaction (game theory), limited information, principal–agent models, human behaviors and preferences, including not only self-interest and risk aversion but also altruism, as well as dynamic processes of change such as creative destruction and instability. Standard tools are taught by showing how they give insight into real-world problems such as inequality and sustainability. The course makes extensive use of data and cutting-edge empirical research.

The course teaches students how economists work:

  • Start with a question, and look at the evidence.
  • Build a model that helps understand what you see.
  • Critically evaluate the model: does it provide insight into the question and explain the evidence?

This course aims to develop students’ analytic approach to, as well as deepen their understanding of, the foundational concepts of microeconomics. It covers consumer and producer theory in-depth and builds up to the analysis of markets. The course will enable students to translate core microeconomic phenomenon into mathematical models, to solve these mathematical models using computation and and graphical tools, and to use these models to analyze the the impact of relevant government policy. It also extends models of microeconomic behavior to cover aspects like behavior under uncertainty, issues of asymmetric information, and market failures.

Note: This course will be offered in 2027-2028 for the first time.

Why are some countries rich while others remain poor? Why do economies grow at different rates, and what explains the large and persistent differences in living standards across the world? These questions lie at the heart of economic growth and development and form the central focus of this course. The course provides an in-depth introduction to the theory and empirics of long-run economic growth, with particular attention to the determinants of cross-country differences in income, productivity, and welfare.


The course combines theoretical models with empirical analysis to examine the principal drivers of economic growth and development. These include physical and human capital accumulation, population dynamics, technological progress, innovation, institutional quality, geography, natural resources, and international economic integration. Throughout the course, theoretical predictions are confronted with real-world evidence, allowing students to assess why some countries have achieved sustained increases in productivity and living standards while others have experienced stagnation, recurrent growth reversals, or persistent poverty.

The main aim of the course is to gain insights into environmental problems from an economic and policy point of view. The course provides an introduction into environmental economics and environmental policy and their application. The central theme is the relationship between society, the economy, and the environment, with application to various themes (e.g. biodiversity conservation, climate change, plastic pollution). We will analyse the mechanisms behind causes of environmental degradation, as well as the effectiveness and efficiency of policy instruments. Problems will be analysed on multiple scales, reaching from the global to local level. During the course, the responsibilities and roles of different actors will be discussed and how they can form obstacles or windows of opportunity for implementing environmental policies. Furthermore, theoretical insights will be applied to contemporary environmental problems.

This course prepares BSc students for a BSc thesis at the ENR group. Students are introduced to the core themes of the ENR group: climate change, social-ecological systems, and environmental-economic behavioural choices. Each theme is dealt with in lectures on the economic theory of the topic and in tutorials or computer practical to practice a quantitative analysis tool for this topic, such as bioeconomic models, statistical analysis, or cost-benefit analysis. In addition students write a literature review on a topic of their own choice, which may or may not be related to any of the three core themes of ENR.

The core themes climate change, social-ecological systems, and environmental-economic behavioural choices are discussed in a theory part and a practice part. The theory part consists of reading material, online knowledge clips, and discussion lectures. The discussion lectures will build on, rather than summarize, the course material so students are expected to prepare for the discussion lecture by studying the reading material and watching the knowledge clips. Reading questions are offered to guide students through the course material, and quizzes to enable students to test their understanding. The practice part entails tutorials with quantitative economic analysis tools. In addition to the lectures and tutorials, students will write a literature review about the economic and environmental literature on a topic of the student's own choice. This could be one of the three themes discussed in the lectures, but students are free to choose another topic. The literature review will be discussed in tutorials where students can compare each other's review and get feedback from their peers and lecturers.

The main topics are categorical data, (multiple) regression, analysis of variance (including multiple comparisons), analysis of covariance, and non-parametric tests. The aims of an analysis, the model assumptions, the properties (and limitations) of the models and associated inferential techniques and the interpretation of results in terms of the practical problem will be discussed. Focus will be upon students gaining an understanding of the model ingredients, an (intuitive) understanding of inferential techniques, insight into data structures and implications for choice of model and analysis. ","type":{"code":"CC","id":"CC","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Continuation courses:"}],"uid":"45f89e4c-ed7e-493b-b499-b4f953a95118"}},{"language":"EN","text":"Climate change and environmental degradation, thousands of migrants who try to cross the Mediterranean on shaky boats, the return of geopolitical conflicts, vast trade agreements that are being negotiated and simultaneously face strong critiques; for many of today's most pressing crises and challenges, citizens, media, and even national politicians look at the European Union institutions for developing effective solutions. Others, on the contrary, blame the European project for being the main reason why these crises have emerged in the first place. In either case, the European Union has a major influence on setting legal frameworks, particularly also in the life sciences domains. The aim of this course is to make students familiar with the basic principles, institutions and policy processes at the EU-level. The course introduces students to the EU's history, its main institutions and legal frameworks, the policymaking process, and the political struggles that take place around a number of policy domains that are relevant to the life sciences.
Although the course is primarily targeted at students of the BSc Economics and Governance (BEB), it is accessible to and insightful for students from different backgrounds who are interested in the basic functioning of the EU and its main policies in the ‘Wageningen domains’. The first half of the course provides a general background to the EU, including its history, main institutions, decision-making procedures, and implementation pathways. In the second half of the course we will discuss the development of a number of relevant policy domains: the internal market, migration policy, marine policy, environmental policy, agricultural policy, and food policy. At the end of the course, students will be able to explain the functioning of the EU’s main institutions and policies, to use and analyze official EU documents and legislation, and to critically appraise an ongoing policy debate.
Beside lectures, the course entails an excursion to Brussels, during which students will experience EU policy-making in real-life. In addition, during the whole course students work on a group paper about an ongoing EU policy debate, such as the Common Agricultural Policy, GMOs, the MERCOSUR trade agreement, the distribution of refugees, or the supervision of banks. However, the call for more and different kinds of policy interventions has become louder. Politicians and citizens demand new types of authorities to control markets, better monitoring systems, and intelligent regulations. These calls are accompanied by new forms of arrangements between government, private enterprises, NGOs, and citizens. With this trend, policy change and governance have become the new 'buzzwords'. Initiatives for policy change and new governance arrangements can stem both from the grass-roots level (bottom up), and from public authorities (top-down). In this course, students learn and apply key theories about how policy change takes place in a dynamic governance context. In so doing, special attention is drawn to theories covering the various stages of the policy process: problem definition, agenda setting, decision making, implementation, and evaluation.

The course covers full working days. Each day consists of three parts: lectures (except for Fridays), group work in tutorials, and independent self-study. During the course, students use the theoretical insights from the literature and the lectures to conduct an in-depth analysis of a specific policy change trajectory in one of the following domains: agriculture, water management, nature conservation and forest management. The analyses are performed in small groups in the afternoons. The four specific policy change trajectories that students can choose from are (i) the EU Common Agricultural Policy, (ii) Room for the River (Ruimte voor de Rivier), (iii) nature conservation in the Oostvaardersplassen, and (iv) forest fires in California, USA. The group work consists of three weekly assignments, which make up fifty (50) percent of the total grade for the course. The course ends with an exam that aids in assessing the students’ understanding of the basic concepts and theoretical perspectives that are discussed in the lectures and literature.

The course is part of the governance track of the Bachelor program Economie en Beleid (BEB; Economics and Governance) and builds on the introductory courses ‘Public Administration and Policy Making’ and ‘Environmental Economics and Environmental Policy’ in year 1. It aims at enhancing the students’ ability to grasp and apply key theoretical public policy and governance concepts and perspectives. Through course materials, lectures and assignments, students are provided with tools to measure and explain income and wealth inequality within and between countries. rich while others have remained poor? Why did the ‘West’ industrialize first? What explains the Asian ‘renaissance’? Why is Latin America caught in a middle-income trap? And will Africa be growing out of poverty in the 21st Century? A deeper understanding of these topics is crucial to make progress on various Sustainable Development Goals, including the worldwide eradication of poverty. Since countries don’t grow rich in a just few years’ time, and poverty doesn’t disappear overnight, answering these big questions requires a long-term perspective. Indeed, the ‘great divergence’ in economic performance and living standards across countries and world regions has a history stretching back for centuries. Economic historians have collected impressive amounts of data to study these divergent experiences. Systematic comparative analyses of historical data has enhanced explanatory models of growth and inequality. In this course we examine the roots of global economic inequality include the role of geography and disease, natural resources, trade, technology, political and social systems, and legal, financial, and commercial institutions. We review the historical evidence on the origins of global economic inequality and links the evidence to a range of economic theories explaining (parts of) the great divergence in income and wealth after 1500.","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"- lectures;

At the essence of spatial and regional economics is that location and distance matter, resulting in interactions in space that can influence various forms of economic activity. For example, firms can change their location and input demand and output supply decisions depending on market conditions and the distance to the relevant input and output markets. Similarly, households can decide on location, consumption and labor supply also depending on spatial factors. Thus, space and its characteristics can influence the choices agents make. What is the best location to start a business? To buy a house? To follow education? To join the labor market? The answer strongly depends on the (expected) costs and benefits of a certain location, as well as the costs and benefits in other locations. Certain places seem to be advantageous to many firms and households and hence, clustering of economic activities takes place.
\tIn this course we focus on two aspects of spatial and regional economics: location theory and regional development.
\tLocation theory deals with location choices of firms and households and the resulting land use. We first start off by examining the behavior of individual firms from a theoretical perspective. This is extended to groups of firms, resulting in agglomeration economies and clustering phenomena. We then look further into the spatial distribution of activities, land use and land markets. This also provides a backbone for analyzing cities and urban-rural interactions. We then extend the analysis to examine regional specialization, trade and multiplier linkages operating between different sectors and regions.
\tThe regional development part focuses on socioeconomic differences within and between regions in both developed and developing countries. We first look into regional and interregional labor market analysis, including the role labor migration plays in the economic adjustment processes of regions. This will include an appraisal of theoretical and empirical insights on regional unemployment disparities. As factor allocation mechanisms across space can influence economic growth, we discuss the nature of regional growth including Keynesian perspectives. Then, regional inequality and policy, as well as wellbeing will be covered. Finally, there will be a discussion on regional voting patterns.
\tThrough a combination of lectures, practicals, excursion, group report and presentation, you will gain knowledge on spatial and regional economic concepts, theories and policy. ","type":{"code":"AK","id":"AK","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Assumed knowledge on:"}],"uid":"fdda01e3-c543-4b24-a3cb-9c4690e5a654"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

The global food system is associated with various issues of sustainability and social justice, from mangrove deforestation in aquaculture, to worker conditions in horticulture, to food deserts in cities. All these issues are about economics – how to organise the food system to meet consumer demands – but they also raise very diverse questions on ethics, power, and environmental sustainability. This diversity of questions and issues requires a similar diversity of perspectives on economics.

This course introduces students to a variety of perspectives on economics, or schools of thought, and discusses their strengths, their weaknesses, and what insights they can give us into the various problems with the food production system. What does Marxist economics have to say about worker conditions in horticulture? How does the view of environmental economists on circular agriculture compare to that of ecological economists? What can we learn from behavioural economics about obesity?

Each week is devoted to a specific theme related to the global food system. This theme is discussed from different economic perspectives in two lectures and one tutorial that takes the form of a debate. Students prepare for the debate by collecting arguments in a group, drawing from the relevant economic schools of thought and other sources.

The transition towards sustainable energy is complex and contested. It involves issues related to international markets, environmental externalities and social and spatial inequalities, and it comes with high economic costs and concerns from diverse stakeholders. While the urgency of transitions is widely acknowledged, there are important decisions to be made: who should take action, which processes and instruments fit best, and how to evaluate policy interventions. What is clear is that the current debate requires well-informed integrated economic and governance insights.

In this course students capitalize on what they have learned in the first two years of the BEB programme and apply their knowledge, methods and skills to problems of energy transitions in the Netherlands, Europe and elsewhere.

Questions that will be explored include: Why do we need an energy transition? What do energy markets currently look like? What market failures prevail? How can we reach acceleration, and facilitate that small scale policy decisions accumulate to large-scale change? What is the stakeholder force field both nationally and internationally? Who is included and excluded in decision-making – and how to come to fair and just policies? What are trade-offs between agglomeration economies and network constraints? Should we account for urban and rural differences? What are the trade-offs between short- and long-term goals, and how we can measure this? What are the main policy controversies and how do they influence the transition? What is the potential for policy interventions?

Education of Public Administration and Policy

The Public Administration and Policy group (PAP) offers a wide range of courses thesis topics and internship opportunities. On this page you will find the information you need for your MSc thesis, internships, research practice and BSc thesis.

Thesis

BSc Thesis

The aim of the BSc thesis is to be able to apply and synthesise knowledge acquired during their education to a demarcated topic. In general a BSc thesis usually consists of formulating a research question, systematically apply research methods, conduct a review of literature on a specific topic and/or applying an existing framework to a case study and writing-up the findings in an accessible and concise report. The student is expected to work individually and should be able to present and defend their findings. PAP is involved in several BSc programs. Contact the BSc coordinator for more information.

Check with your study advisor for the most up to date BSc thesis documents.

Documents

  • BSc Thesis course guide
  • BSc Thesis intake form
  • BIN Thesis contract

MSc Thesis

The thesis is the crown on your Master's degree program. For the course guide, assessment form and rubric of the MSc thesis, please consult this page.

For specific information about doing a Master Thesis at our group, please read the MSc Thesis Course Guide. Part A of this guide gives you information about MSc theses at WU and part B contains the WCSG chair group specific regulations (ENP/PAP).

New MSc students looking for a PAP supervisor can sign up by sending this form to office.pap@wur.nl.

For the most up to date documents, please consult this page (login required).

Internship & Research practice

The aim of the internship, in general, is to work in and for an organization where you can use and develop your analytical tools and skills and to experience challenges and everyday practices of researchers, consultants and civil servants. We have collaborative relationships with various public and private organizations that regularly offer internship possibilities for PAP students.

If you are interested in doing an internship with one of these organizations, you can approach Dr Siera Vercillo (MME) or Dr Otto Hospes (MID). Please regularly check our website for new internship possibilities.

Going abroad: If you are planning to go abroad for thesis/internship related activities, make sure to check out the WUR travel policy and the preparation page (you can also find the forms for travelling there). How to register your travels in Osiris you can find here. Note that for some countries you will have to ask for approval first.

For the most up to date documents, please consult this page (login required).
